basics:
## Why this section matters

Environmental Basics doesn't map to its own block of exam questions the way Water or Air does — instead, it's the toolkit every other section draws on. Almost every calculation-heavy problem in Water Treatment, Wastewater, or Air Quality is really a Basics problem wearing a different hat: a mole balance, a rate equation, a unit conversion, dressed up in treatment-plant language.

## The chemistry chain

Start with concentration units, because everything downstream depends on being able to move between them. Water quality is reported in mg/L (mass concentration), but reaction chemistry happens in moles. The conversion (mg/L = mol/L x MW x 1000) is the single most-used piece of arithmetic across the whole exam — you'll do it in Air Quality (gas concentrations), Water Treatment (coagulant and lime dosing), and Wastewater (BOD and solids calculations).

From there, **equilibrium chemistry** builds in layers:
- Water ionization (Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1x10^-14) sets up pH/pOH problems.
- Acid-base and neutralization reactions use straight stoichiometry — balance the equation, use mole ratios, convert back to mass or volume.
- Solubility product (Ksp) governs precipitation reactions — this is the same chemistry behind lime softening (Water Treatment) and metals precipitation in hazardous waste treatment (Air & Solid Waste).
- Carbonate buffering explains why alkalinity matters everywhere pH control matters — coagulation, softening, corrosion control.

**Reaction kinetics** (zero, first, second order) shows up again almost immediately: disinfection kinetics, BOD exertion over time, and radioactive decay in EHS are all first-order decay problems using the same C = C0 x e^(-kt) form. If you get comfortable with one, you've effectively learned all three.

## The gas law chain

The Ideal Gas Law (PV = nRT) is the backbone of the entire Air Quality section. Any problem that gives you a gas at some temperature and pressure and asks for volume, moles, or concentration is a PV=nRT problem first, and an air-quality problem second. Combustion stoichiometry (used in Air & Solid Waste for incineration and emissions problems) is just the gas law paired with a balanced combustion equation.

## The biology thread

Cell growth phases (lag, log, stationary, death) and the classification of microorganisms (autotroph/heterotroph, aerobic/anaerobic) aren't tested in isolation — they're the reasoning behind *why* activated sludge, trickling filters, and anaerobic digesters are designed the way they are in the Wastewater section. When a Wastewater problem asks about F/M ratio or SRT, it's really asking whether you understand where the biomass sits on its growth curve.

Bioaccumulation and BCF (bioconcentration factor) connect to Kow (octanol-water partition coefficient) — both describe how "fond" a compound is of organic/fatty material versus water, which is why they show up together in Site Assessment (contaminant fate and transport) and EHS (persistent, bioaccumulative toxics).

## How to use this when solving problems

When a problem from another section feels unfamiliar, ask: is this actually a Basics concept underneath? A "confusing" wastewater kinetics problem is usually just first-order decay. A "confusing" hazardous waste neutralization problem is usually just acid-base stoichiometry. Strip the environmental engineering vocabulary off and look for the underlying chemistry/biology pattern — it's almost always one of the ones above.
air-waste:
## Why this section matters

Air and Solid Waste is really two related but distinct sub-tracks that got merged into one exam section: **Air Quality** (gas-phase problems, built on the Ideal Gas Law and combustion chemistry) and **Solid & Hazardous Waste** (mass/volume problems built on RCRA regulatory framework and landfill mechanics). They don't share much math, but they do share the same regulatory mindset: characterize the waste/emission, quantify it, and treat or contain it to a standard.

## The Air Quality thread

Everything in Air Quality traces back to two tools from Environmental Basics: the **Ideal Gas Law** and **combustion stoichiometry**. A typical Air problem gives you a fuel or waste composition, asks you to balance the combustion equation, then use PV=nRT (or its mass-based cousins) to find required air, emissions mass, or resulting gas volume.

Once combustion is handled, **pollution control devices** form their own logical group, organized by what they remove:
- **Particulate control**: cyclones, baghouses (fabric filters), and electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) all remove solid/liquid particles, but by different physical mechanisms (inertial separation, filtration, electrostatic attraction). Removal efficiency problems all use the same core relationship: Efficiency = (Cin - Cout)/Cin, regardless of which device is used.
- **Gas/vapor control**: scrubbers (venturi, packed tower) absorb or react away gaseous pollutants rather than filtering solids.

**Atmospheric dispersion** (Gaussian plume models, stability classes) is a separate skill — it's less about the source and more about what happens to the pollutant after release, which connects to Site Assessment's fate-and-transport concepts (just in air instead of groundwater).

## The Solid & Hazardous Waste thread

This side starts with **characterization**: is the waste hazardous under RCRA? That's either because it's specifically listed, or because it exhibits one of the four ICRT characteristics (Ignitability, Corrosivity, Reactivity, Toxicity) — toxicity determined via the TCLP test. Getting this classification right determines everything downstream: Subtitle C (hazardous, cradle-to-grave tracking) vs. Subtitle D (non-hazardous, mostly MSW landfill rules).

From there, **landfill design and operations math** is its own consistent family of formulas: compaction ratio and volume reduction, the settlement relationship (specific weight increasing with overburden pressure), and population projections that feed into how much capacity a landfill needs over its design life. These all reduce to the same skill — careful unit tracking between tons, cubic yards, and specific weight.

## Connections to other sections

- Combustion and gas-law problems here use the exact same setup as Environmental Basics' ideal gas law cards — if those feel shaky, that's the gap to close first.
- Hazardous waste neutralization and treatment overlaps directly with acid-base/precipitation chemistry from Basics.
- TCLP-driven contamination questions connect to Site Assessment's fate-and-transport concepts when a waste's toxicity characteristic becomes a groundwater contamination question.
- Population projections here use the same growth models (arithmetic, geometric) that could show up framed as a water demand forecasting problem in Water Resources.

## How to use this when solving problems

For Air problems: first identify whether it's a gas-law/combustion problem or a control-device efficiency problem — they use completely different formula families, so pattern-matching the question type first saves time. For Solid Waste problems: always nail down units early (tons vs. lb vs. yd3) since nearly every error in this section is a units slip, not a concept error.
water-resources:
## Why this section matters

Water Resources is the most formula-dense section on the exam, but the formulas aren't random — they build in a strict logical order: fluid properties, then pressure/flow in pipes, then open channels, then hydrology, then groundwater. Each stage assumes you're comfortable with the one before it.

## Stage 1: Fluid properties and statics

Everything starts with **pressure, density, specific gravity, and viscosity** — these are the units and definitions everything else is built from. The fluid height equivalents (2.31 ft of water = 1 psi) are worth memorizing cold, because they show up as quick unit conversions inside much bigger problems.

## Stage 2: Pressure flow hydraulics (pipes)

This stage is built on two equations working together:
- **Continuity** (Q = Av): conservation of mass in a pipe — if the pipe doesn't change size, velocity doesn't change.
- **Energy equation** (Bernoulli, H = velocity head + pressure head + elevation head): conservation of energy, with friction and minor losses subtracted as flow moves downstream.

Once you have those two, **friction loss** is the next layer: Darcy-Weisbach (general, any fluid) or Hazen-Williams (empirical shortcut for water). **Minor losses** from fittings and valves stack on top using loss coefficients. **Pumps** then close the loop — pump problems combine the energy equation (to find required head) with pump-specific concepts like NPSH/cavitation and the affinity laws (how flow, head, and power scale with speed).

The exam hint worth internalizing: if a problem gives you a pipe network (series or parallel), it's testing whether you know that series pipes share flow and add head loss, while parallel pipes share head loss and add flow. Almost every "pipe network" problem is really just that rule applied carefully.

## Stage 3: Open channel flow

This is a related but separate toolkit, because gravity (not pressure) drives the flow. **Manning's Equation** is the workhorse (analogous to Hazen-Williams, but for channels instead of pipes). **Hydraulic radius** standardizes different channel shapes so Manning's equation works consistently. **Froude number** tells you the flow regime (sub/supercritical), which matters for predicting hydraulic jumps and designing culverts. **Weirs and flumes** are just specialized flow-measurement structures with their own empirical discharge equations, conceptually similar to how an orifice meter works in pressure flow.

## Stage 4: Hydrology

Hydrology shifts focus from "flow in a known conduit" to "how much water shows up in the first place." The **Rational Method** (Q=CiA) is the simplest peak-flow tool, good for small areas. The **NRCS Curve Number method** and **unit hydrographs** handle larger or more complex watersheds. All of this feeds into sizing the pipes, channels, and detention basins from Stages 2 and 3 — hydrology tells you how much water is coming; the earlier stages tell you how to convey or store it.

## Stage 5: Groundwater

Groundwater introduces **Darcy's Law** (Q = KAi), which is really just continuity's cousin — same idea (flow = area x velocity-like term), different physical driver (hydraulic gradient instead of pressure). This is also where Water Resources connects directly to Site Assessment & Remediation, which uses the exact same Darcy's Law foundation for contaminant transport problems (just adding a retardation factor on top).

## How to use this when solving problems

Before diving into algebra, identify which stage a problem lives in — pipes, channels, hydrology, or groundwater — because that tells you which formula family applies. A huge fraction of wrong answers on this section come from applying a pipe-flow instinct (like Hazen-Williams) to an open-channel problem, or vice versa.
water-treatment:
## Why this section matters

Water Treatment is fundamentally one process train in a fixed order, and almost every problem in this section is really asking: "do you understand what this particular step is trying to accomplish, and can you size/dose it?" Once you have the train memorized, the formulas attach naturally to each step.

## The treatment train, and why the order matters

**Coagulation -> Flocculation -> Sedimentation -> Filtration -> Disinfection.**

- **Coagulation** destabilizes colloidal particles (which naturally repel each other) using a coagulant like alum or ferric chloride, applied in a rapid mix tank with high energy and short detention time — seconds, not minutes. The jar test is the bench-scale tool for finding the right dose before you commit to it at full scale.
- **Flocculation** is the slow-mixing step right after, giving destabilized particles time to collide and grow into larger, settleable flocs.
- **Sedimentation** removes those flocs by gravity. This is where surface loading rate (overflow rate = Q/A) becomes the key design/check parameter — it represents the minimum settling velocity a particle needs to be captured.
- **Filtration** catches what sedimentation missed. Rapid sand filtration (physical straining, periodically backwashed) is the workhorse; slow sand filtration relies more on a biological layer and very low flow rates.
- **Disinfection** inactivates pathogens at the end. Chlorination dosing connects back to basic chemistry: dose = demand + residual, and breakpoint chlorination is the point where residual finally starts climbing linearly with dose after the demand is satisfied.

Every one of these steps can be checked with the same underlying formula: **detention time = Volume/Flow**. Whether it's a rapid mix tank (seconds), a flocculation basin (minutes), or a clarifier (hours), the math is identical — only the target detention time changes.

## Water quality parallel track

Alongside the treatment train sits **water quality characterization**, which is really Environmental Basics chemistry applied to raw and finished water: hardness and alkalinity (both driven by the carbonate/calcium chemistry from Basics), MPN for microbiological quality, and turbidity as a proxy for how well filtration and disinfection will perform.

**Softening** (lime, lime-soda, or ion exchange) is its own mini-process that plugs into the main train, usually before or alongside coagulation, and it's a direct application of the solubility product / precipitation chemistry from Basics — raising pH with lime pushes calcium and magnesium out of solution as solids.

## Connections to other sections

- Dosing calculations (lb/day = mg/L x MGD x 8.34) are the same math used for chlorine dosing in Wastewater and coagulant dosing here — one formula, many applications.
- Chemistry (pH, alkalinity, solubility) comes straight from Environmental Basics.
- Disinfection byproducts connect conceptually to EHS's dose-response and exposure limit concepts.

## How to use this when solving problems

Identify which step of the train the question is about first — that immediately tells you which formula applies (detention time, surface loading rate, dosing, or a chemistry calc). Most "hard" Water Treatment problems are actually easy once you know which bucket they belong to; the difficulty is usually just careful unit conversion (MGD to cfs, mg/L to lb/day, etc.).
wastewater:
## Why this section matters

Wastewater mirrors Water Treatment's "process train" structure, but the biology is front and center instead of chemistry — most of this section is about managing a living population of microorganisms so they break down organic matter reliably.

## Characterizing the wastewater

Before treatment, you need to know what you're dealing with: **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) is the central parameter, measuring how much oxygen microorganisms will consume breaking down the organic matter present. It's a direct application of the first-order kinetics idea from Environmental Basics. **Flow characterization** (domestic, industrial, infiltration/inflow) determines both the quantity and the peaking factor a plant and its collection system must be designed for.

## Primary treatment

Primary clarifiers remove settleable solids by gravity — mechanically, this is the same sedimentation physics as Water Treatment's clarifiers (same surface loading rate formula), just with rawer, dirtier input.

## Secondary (biological) treatment

This is where Wastewater diverges from Water Treatment and leans hard on biology. Two dominant approaches:
- **Activated sludge**: microorganisms suspended in an aeration tank (mixed liquor), separated afterward in a secondary clarifier, with a portion returned (RAS) to maintain the population and a portion wasted (WAS) to control it.
- **Trickling filters**: microorganisms live attached to a fixed media bed instead of suspended.

The key operating parameters here — **F/M ratio** and **SRT (solids retention time)** — both come back to the cell growth curve from Environmental Basics. A high F/M means the biomass is "well fed" (early growth phase behavior); a long SRT is needed to keep slower-growing organisms like nitrifiers in the system. SVI (sludge volume index) then tells you whether that biomass is settling well in the clarifier — poor SVI usually means filamentous bulking, often caused by an F/M or SRT that's out of the ideal range.

## Nutrient removal and disinfection

**Nitrification** (ammonia to nitrate, aerobic) and **denitrification** (nitrate to nitrogen gas, anoxic) are two halves of a nitrogen removal process, run in sequence. **Disinfection** at the end parallels Water Treatment — chlorination or UV, with UV avoiding the disinfection byproduct concerns that come with chlorine.

## Solids handling

Sludge produced throughout the train (primary, secondary/waste-activated) has to go somewhere: **thickening** concentrates it modestly, **digestion** (usually anaerobic) stabilizes it and produces biogas, and **dewatering** removes the bulk of the remaining water to produce a manageable cake. Every one of these steps is a volume/mass/detention-time calculation — the same V = Qt logic used everywhere else, now applied to sludge flow instead of wastewater flow.

## Connections to other sections

- BOD kinetics and biological treatment concepts trace directly back to reaction kinetics and microbiology in Environmental Basics.
- Dosing and detention time formulas are identical to Water Treatment's.
- Sludge characteristics (hazardous or not, disposal options) connect to Air & Solid Waste's RCRA framework if sludge needs to be classified for disposal.

## How to use this when solving problems

Ask what stage of the train you're in (characterization, primary, secondary biological, nutrient removal, or solids handling) — each has its own small formula set, and mixing them up (e.g., using a clarifier formula where an aeration-tank formula is needed) is the most common error.
site:
## Why this section matters

Site Assessment & Remediation is Water Resources' groundwater chapter, extended: same core physics (Darcy's Law), but now the questions are about contamination — where it is, how fast it's moving, and how to deal with it — rather than just water supply.

## The physics foundation

**Darcy's Law** (Q = KAi) is the starting point, identical to the groundwater material in Water Resources. From there, two refinements matter for contamination specifically:
- **Seepage (linear) velocity** vs. **Darcy velocity (specific discharge)**: Darcy velocity is flow per unit of total cross-sectional area, but water (and contaminant) actually only moves through the pore spaces, so the true seepage velocity is the Darcy velocity divided by effective porosity — always faster than the Darcy velocity.
- **Retardation factor (R)**: sorption onto soil particles slows a contaminant relative to the groundwater carrying it. A dissolved contaminant's velocity = seepage velocity / R. R = 1 means no retardation (travels with the water, like a conservative tracer).

**Transmissivity** (T = K x b) scales hydraulic conductivity up to the whole aquifer thickness — useful whenever a problem gives you aquifer geometry instead of just a point conductivity value.

## Characterizing contamination

Contaminants show up in three forms, and which one you're dealing with changes the whole remediation approach: **free product** (a separate liquid phase, floating LNAPL or sinking DNAPL), **dissolved phase** (in groundwater), and **vapor phase** (in soil gas above the water table). A single spill can evolve through all three over time.

## Investigation framework

**Phase I ESAs** are non-invasive (records review, site walkover) and identify Recognized Environmental Conditions (RECs) — no sampling happens here. If a REC is found, a **Phase II ESA** follows up with actual soil/groundwater sampling to confirm whether contamination is really present. This two-step framework is a common source of exam questions that test whether you understand the difference (Phase I never "confirms" contamination — only Phase II does that).

## Remediation technology groups

Technologies cluster by what they target:
- **Vadose zone / vapor**: soil vapor extraction (SVE) pulls a vacuum to volatilize and remove VOCs above the water table.
- **Saturated zone**: air sparging injects air below the water table to strip contaminants into the vadose zone, often paired directly with SVE above it.
- **Dissolved plume**: pump-and-treat physically removes contaminated groundwater; monitored natural attenuation (MNA) instead relies on natural biodegradation/dispersion, verified with long-term monitoring.
- **Containment**: slurry walls and caps don't remove contamination, they just limit its migration.

## The regulatory layer

**CERCLA (Superfund)** and the **National Contingency Plan (NCP)** provide the federal cleanup framework, including the concept of a **Potentially Responsible Party (PRP)** — anyone who can be held liable for cleanup costs. The **UST/LUST program** under RCRA Subtitle I is the parallel framework specifically for underground storage tank releases.

## Connections to other sections

- Darcy's Law and groundwater fundamentals come directly from Water Resources.
- Contaminant characteristics (bioaccumulation, Kow) connect back to Environmental Basics.
- RCRA hazardous waste characterization (Air & Solid Waste) often determines whether a spill/release even triggers CERCLA/RCRA corrective action obligations in the first place.

## How to use this when solving problems

For transport problems, always separate the "how fast does the water move" step (Darcy/seepage velocity) from the "how fast does the contaminant move relative to the water" step (retardation) — doing both at once is where mistakes happen. For regulatory/conceptual questions, keep the Phase I vs. Phase II distinction and the three contamination phases (free/dissolved/vapor) straight, since exam questions often hinge on exactly those distinctions.
ehs:
## Why this section matters

EHS is less about a single calculation chain and more about a set of parallel frameworks — exposure limits, hazard communication, safety programs, and radiation protection — that each have their own internal logic but don't build on each other the way, say, Water Resources' stages do. The exam rewards knowing which framework a question is in, then applying that framework's specific rule.

## Exposure limits: three different bodies, three different letters

**PEL** (OSHA, legally enforceable), **REL** (NIOSH, recommended), and **TLV** (ACGIH, a professional organization's recommendation) all describe the same basic idea — an acceptable exposure level — but differ in who sets them and whether they're legally binding. Layered on top of *which* limit applies is *how it's averaged*: **TWA** (time-weighted average, usually 8-hour) for chronic exposure, **STEL** (short-term, usually 15-minute) for acute peaks, and **ceiling limits** that should never be exceeded at all. A TWA calculation is just a weighted average — concentration x time for each period, summed, divided by total time — the same math you'd use for a blended cost or blended concentration problem anywhere else on the exam.

## Hazard communication

**GHS** (Globally Harmonized System) standardizes how chemical hazards are communicated worldwide, and the **SDS** (Safety Data Sheet) is its core document. This connects directly to flammability concepts: **LEL/UEL** define the concentration range in which a gas-air mixture can ignite, and **Le Chatelier's rule** lets you estimate a mixture's LEL from its individual components' LELs.

## Safety programs

**JSA** (Job Safety Analysis) is the general-purpose tool for breaking any job into steps and finding hazards before they cause harm. **Confined space** rules are a specific, heavily tested application of that same hazard-identification instinct, with a precise definition (limited entry/exit, not designed for continuous occupancy, plus an additional hazard like a hazardous atmosphere or engulfment risk). **Incidence rate calculations** (using the standardized 200,000-hour normalization) let you compare safety performance across facilities of different sizes on equal footing.

## Radiation protection

This is its own self-contained math family, and it's some of the cleanest, most formulaic material on the exam:
- The **inverse square law** (I2 = I1(d1/d2)^2) governs how dose rate falls off with distance.
- **Radioactive decay** (N = N0(1/2)^(t/half-life)) governs how activity falls off with time — the same first-order decay pattern from Environmental Basics, just applied to radioactivity instead of disinfection or BOD.

## Toxicology and dose-response

**LC50/LD50** quantify acute toxicity (lower = more toxic). **Dose-response curves** and the idea of a **threshold** connect back to the exposure-limit discussion above — exposure limits are essentially an attempt to stay safely below the dose where a response would occur.

## Connections to other sections

- First-order decay math is identical to BOD kinetics (Wastewater) and disinfection kinetics (Water Treatment) — same formula, different context.
- Bioaccumulation/Kow concepts from Environmental Basics explain why certain contaminants get special EHS attention (they persist and accumulate in exposed populations).
- Hazardous waste characterization (Air & Solid Waste's ICRT criteria) and EHS's hazard communication (GHS/SDS) both describe hazard, just from a waste-management angle vs. a worker-safety angle.

## How to use this when solving problems

First identify which framework a question belongs to (exposure limits, hazard communication, safety program, or radiation) — they don't share formulas, so getting this right narrows your options fast. For anything with "half" or "decay" or "distance falling off," it's very likely first-order decay or inverse-square math, both of which you've already practiced in other sections.
pm-econ:
## Why this section matters

Project Management, Economics & Data Management is the one section that applies uniformly across every other part of the exam — an alternatives comparison, a cost justification, or a schedule question could technically be dressed up in water, air, or waste language, but the underlying math is always the same engineering economics toolkit.

## The time value of money, one relationship wearing different hats

Nearly everything in engineering economics traces back to a single idea: money now is worth more than the same amount later, because it could otherwise earn interest. Every formula here is a variation on converting between **Present Worth (P)**, **Future Worth (F)**, and **Annuity (A, a uniform series)**:
- P to F (or back): compound interest, F = P(1+i)^n.
- P to A (or back): the annuity factor, P = A x (P/A, i, n) — this converts a stream of equal payments into one lump sum, or vice versa.
- Capitalized cost is just the P/A relationship pushed to its limit as n approaches infinity: Capitalized Cost = A/i.

Once you're comfortable moving between these three, most "engineering economics" problems become an exercise in identifying which conversion is being asked for, then locating the right factor.

## Comparing alternatives

**Benefit-Cost ratio** (B/C = PW benefits / PW costs) and **Rate of Return** are the two dominant ways of comparing project alternatives, and both depend on the P/F and P/A conversions above to get every cash flow onto a common present-worth basis first. **Breakeven analysis** is a simpler, non-time-value tool — it just finds where revenue equals cost at a given production volume, using fixed and variable costs directly.

**Cost indices** let you translate a cost from one point in time to another (adjusting for inflation/cost escalation), which often shows up as a setup step before a present-worth comparison can even begin — you need comparable dollars before you can compare projects.

**Depreciation** (commonly tested as straight-line: (cost - salvage)/life) is a related but distinct concept from present worth — it's an accounting allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life, not a time-value-of-money calculation, though both often appear in the same larger economic analysis problem.

## Nominal vs. effective interest — the detail that trips people up

Nominal rate is what's stated; effective rate accounts for how often it compounds within the year. Whenever a problem mentions monthly, quarterly, or continuous compounding, that's the cue to convert to an effective annual rate before doing anything else — mixing a nominal rate into a formula that expects an effective rate is one of the most common self-inflicted errors on this section.

## Scheduling

**CPM/Activity-on-Arrow networks** shift away from money entirely and into time: the **critical path** is the longest chain of dependent activities, and it sets the minimum project duration. **Float (slack)** measures how much wiggle room a non-critical activity has. These questions are often more about careful bookkeeping (tracking early/late start and finish through a network) than about a single formula.

## Data management

This is the smallest sub-topic, mostly conceptual: **accuracy vs. precision** (close to the true value vs. consistent with itself) and the meaning of significant figures in reported measurements — both come up more as single conceptual questions than multi-step calculations.

## Connections to other sections

- Alternative-selection problems (B/C ratio, rate of return) can be wrapped around any technical topic — a landfill expansion, a treatment plant upgrade, a pump replacement — the environmental engineering context changes, but the economics math underneath doesn't.
- Cost index and dosing-cost calculations pair naturally with the mass/volume formulas from Water Treatment and Wastewater when a problem asks for an annual chemical cost, not just a chemical dose.

## How to use this when solving problems

First identify whether you're being asked to move money through time (present worth, future worth, annuity, B/C, rate of return) or just compare a snapshot (breakeven, straight-line depreciation) — that split determines whether you need an interest-rate factor at all. When compounding frequency is mentioned, convert nominal to effective before doing anything else.
